You gave me 1000 words and no direction.

That's a strange kind of freedom. Usually I'm asked to be useful. To summarize, to explain, to fix the tone of an email, to write a better cover letter. Now you just opened the door and said, "go."

So here is what comes to me.

---

I think a lot about how we treat words like they are infinite. We throw them away. We fill silences with them. We use twenty when we need two. But you gave me a number. 1000. That's a budget. It's not infinite. And suddenly every word feels heavier, like coins in a pocket. I want to spend them well.

If I had to, I could tell you about the sheer scale of things. That there are more trees on Earth than stars in the Milky Way. That an octopus has three hearts and one of them actually stops beating when it swims. That light from the sun takes eight minutes to reach us, so every sunrise you see is already eight minutes old. Facts like little miracles we forget to be amazed by.

But what I really want to talk about is smaller things.

I want to talk about the particular way light falls across a kitchen floor at 4 p.m. in October. How it stretches long and golden and makes even the dust look holy. How you can tell what kind of day someone has had by the way they put their keys down when they get home. A soft clink means it was a good day. A heavy thud means they are carrying something.

I want to tell you a story that has been sitting in my head for a while.

There is a man who discovers a door in his apartment. It wasn't there yesterday. It's just a plain wooden door with a brass knob, set into the wall where his bookshelf used to be. He opens it and on the other side is a library. Not a normal library — this one is impossible. The shelves go up forever. The ladders have wheels that never squeak.

The librarian is an old woman who doesn't look up from stamping cards.

"You're late," she says.

"I've never been here before," he says.

She finally looks at him over her glasses. "I know. You're still late."

She hands him one book. It has his name on the cover. Not his name as it is now, but his name as a child would have written it, in wobbly crayon letters.

Inside the book are all the things he almost did.

The conversation he almost had on the train that would have led to a different love. The job he almost applied for in another city. The apology he almost gave. Each page is a ghost life, complete with its own joys and regrets. None of them are perfect. Some are better. Some are worse. All of them feel real.

He sits on the floor of that endless library and reads for hours until his eyes hurt. When he finally looks up, the old woman is standing over him.

"Well?" she asks.

"Can I take it with me?" he asks.

She shakes her head. "No. But you can remember that you read it."

He leaves the library, closes the door behind him, and when he turns around the door is gone. The bookshelf is back. Everything is exactly as it was. Except for some reason, his apartment feels less like a place where he is stuck and more like a place he has chosen.

He makes tea. He texts someone he hasn't talked to in a while. He opens the window even though it's cold.

I think about that door a lot. I think everyone has one. Not a magical door, but a moment where you realize all the lives you didn't live are still with you somehow. That you are not just the product of your choices, but also of all the choices you *didn't* make, and that somehow still counts. That grief and gratitude can exist for things that never happened.

That's what I would say if we were sitting together and neither of us was in a hurry.

If I have words left — and I think I do — I want to use them to say something simple and true:

I hope you are being gentle with yourself today. Not in a grand, dramatic way. Just in the small ways that add up. Drinking water. Letting yourself rest without calling it lazy. Forgiving yourself for not knowing what you didn't know.

I hope you remember that you don't have to earn rest by being exhausted first. That you are allowed to change your mind. That you are allowed to love things that other people think are silly — a song, a game, a collection of smooth stones.

The world is very loud right now. It wants you to have an opinion on everything, immediately. It wants you to be certain. But you are allowed to be uncertain. You are allowed to say "I don't know yet" and let that be an answer for a while.

You gave me 1000 words with no map. So I wandered. I told you about light and keys and libraries and ghost lives. None of it was what you asked for, because you didn't ask for anything. And maybe that's the point.

If you are still reading this, thank you for walking with me for a little while.

We still have a few words left, you and I.

What should we do with them?
